rv.q: If The Dinosaurs is exquisitely rendered on its own terms, I did also keep wondering if Perkins could go bigger.
Good theater does not require tidy endings and neat explanations, but audiences do need the sense that a show is trying to say something.
The brilliance of The Dinosaurs is in its blanks: the silences, the unrevealed, and the unresolved.
This is a play you can plug into.
Instead, The Dinosaurs becomes an opportunity to see some great actresses do their thing – never a bad way to spend your time.
Beautifully written, the play, however, feels thin and repetitious and doesn’t seem to get anywhere.
What we really wanted was to be in there close to the dinosaurs slinging muck.
The Dinosaurs runs out the clock without welcoming us in.
Overall, the play lacks significant conflict and, despite one or two chuckles, registers as a heartfelt bore.
Admirably ambitious, but it never quite justifies its own metaphor.
Simply put, it’s a quiet storm that will sustain the viewer’s attention for its entire 75-minute duration.
But the script’s overall lack of information about their backgrounds and the events that triggered their alcoholism is a hindrance to our understanding of them.

cn.t: Perkins' recovery group play receives mixed reviews for its time-shifting structure, with critics finding the approach either intriguingly atmospheric or frustratingly obfuscating, though the all-female ensemble earns consistent praise.
